title: Scyld the Founder and His Heir
summary: A narrator's prelude praises Scyld Scefing, a foundling who seized the mead-benches of rival tribes, became a tribute-taking king, and fathered a renowned son, Beowulf of the Scandian lands.

title: Scyld's Ship Funeral at Sea
summary: Scyld dies at his appointed hour, and his grieving clansmen, following his own command, lay him in a ship heaped with weapons and treasure under a gold banner and give him to the ocean, with no one able to say who receives him.

title: The Scyldings' Line Through Healfdene
summary: The poet traces the Scylding line from Beowulf through Healfdene to his four children, Heorogar, Hrothgar, Halga and a daughter who became a queen, and notes that Hrothgar's martial glory won his kin's obedience until his warband grew great.

title: Hrothgar Raises the Hall Heorot
summary: Hrothgar, grown mighty with a loyal warband, orders a vast mead-hall built, names it Heorot, and gives out rings and treasure at its feasts, while the poet foretells that fire and a feud between father and son-in-law will come.

title: Grendel Hears the Singing
summary: From his dark dwelling, a spirit consumed by envy and anger hears the daily harp-music and the singer's song of creation echoing from Heorot, while the poet notes the clansmen's happy life lasting until one began to fashion evils.

title: Grendel and Cain's Kin
summary: The poet names the spirit in the dark as Grendel, a march-stepper of the moors and fens, descended from Cain, whose kin God banished from men for Abel's slaying, along with all the monstrous giants, elves and evil spirits who warred with God and were repaid.

title: Grendel Raids Heorot by Night
summary: At nightfall Grendel enters Heorot, finds the feasted Danes asleep and unwary, seizes thirty thanes, and carries their bodies back to his lair.

title: Grendel's Reign of Terror
summary: At dawn the Danes discover Grendel's slaughter and Hrothgar sits grieving, then Grendel's killing resumes the next night, driving survivors to sleep far from the hall until Heorot stands empty for a long time.

title: Twelve Years of Hrothgar's Sorrow
summary: For twelve years Hrothgar endures Grendel's unrelenting raids, which are known far and wide in song, while Grendel rejects any peace or payment and Heorot stays unusable to its king.

title: The Danes Pray to Idols
summary: Grieving Hrothgar and his assembled nobles seek counsel against Grendel and, ignorant of the true God, vow offerings in heathen shrines to beg the slayer-of-souls for help, while the poet laments the damned and blesses those who find the Lord.

title: Beowulf Sails to Danish Shores
summary: Hearing of Grendel's raids, Hygelac's thane Beowulf has a ship readied to aid the Danish king, chooses fourteen of the keenest Geats, sails two days, and lands on the Danish coast, thanking God for a safe crossing.

title: The Warden Challenges the Geats
summary: A Danish coast-warden watching from the cliff sees armed strangers unloading shields and gear from a ship, rides down to the shore brandishing his spear, and demands to know who they are, warning that they lack the Danes' leave to land and must declare their origin quickly or be taken for spies, while remarking on the striking presence of one of the company.

title: The Geats Declare Their Errand
summary: Beowulf declares to the coast-warden that he is Ecgtheow's son and Hygelac's thane, come in good faith to aid Hrothgar against the night-raiding monster, and the warden accepts his sincerity, guides the Geats inland, and posts guards over their ship.

title: The Geats March to Heorot
summary: Beowulf and his Geats march in armor beneath boar-crested helms, leaving their anchored ship guarded, until they sight Heorot's gold-bright gables, where the coast-warden points out the hall, blesses them, and rides back to his seaward watch.

title: The Geats Reach Hrothgar's Hall
summary: The Geats stack their shields and spears against Heorot's wall, and Hrothgar's herald Wulfgar questions their origin; Beowulf names himself as Hygelac's follower and asks to speak with Hrothgar, and Wulfgar agrees to carry the request to the king and return with his answer.

title: Wulfgar Announces the Geats
summary: Wulfgar goes to Hrothgar's side and announces that Geats led by Beowulf have crossed the sea, asks the king to grant them an audience, and vouches for their worthiness and their leader.

title: Hrothgar Recalls Ecgtheow's Son
summary: Hrothgar recalls Beowulf's father Ecgtheow and the Geatish marriage tie, repeats the seamen's report of Beowulf's thirty-man grip, takes him as God-sent against Grendel, and orders Wulfgar to bring the Geats in as welcome guests.

title: Wulfgar Bids the Geats Enter
summary: Wulfgar returns to the hall door and tells the Geats that Hrothgar welcomes them, permitting them to enter in armor and helmets but requiring that shields and spears be left outside; Beowulf rises, leaves some thanes guarding the gear, and leads the rest behind Wulfgar into Heorot toward the hearth.

title: Beowulf's Vow to Purge Heorot
summary: Standing before Hrothgar in gleaming mail, Beowulf recounts his past feats, asks leave to purge Heorot alone with his Geats, vows to fight Grendel bare-handed since the monster uses no weapons, and instructs that his mail be sent to Hygelac should he die.

title: Hrothgar Recounts the Feud and Grendel
summary: Hrothgar answers Beowulf's vow by recalling how he settled Ecgtheow's feud with the Wylfings with treasure, laments the warriors Grendel has taken after their drunken boasts of standing against him, describes the blood-soaked hall each morning, and invites Beowulf to sit and feast and speak freely.

title: The Geats Feast in Heorot
summary: The Geats take their assigned benches in Heorot, a henchman pours clear mead, minstrels sing, and Danes and Geats revel together in the hall.

title: Unferth Taunts Beowulf Over Breca
summary: Unferth, envious of Beowulf's fame, interrupts the feast to taunt him with the tale of his lost swimming contest against Breca and predicts a worse fate if he waits for Grendel through the night.

title: Beowulf's Boast of the Sea
summary: Beowulf answers the drunken Unferth by claiming he outlasted Breca in a boyhood sea-swim, recounting five nights in the freezing surf, his mail saving him from a sea-beast's grip, and his killing the monster with his sword.

title: Beowulf Concludes His Swimming Boast
summary: Beowulf finishes his sea-tale, claiming he slew nine sea-monsters and washed ashore in Finland, then turns on Unferth as a kinslayer whose cowardice let Grendel rampage, and vows to fight Grendel at dawn; Hrothgar is heartened, the hall laughs, and Queen Wealhtheow enters and offers the cup first to Hrothgar.

title: The Queen's Cup, Hrothgar's Charge
summary: Wealhtheow thanks God and hands Beowulf the cup, he swears to free the Danes or die in the hall, and at nightfall Hrothgar hands Heorot's watch to him for the first time to any man.

title: The Hall Is Left to Beowulf
summary: Hrothgar leaves Heorot to seek Wealhtheow, and Beowulf doffs his mail and helmet, hands his sword to a henchman, repeats his vow to meet Grendel unarmed and leave the verdict to God, then lies down among his Geats, who expect never to see home again while the narrator hints that God will grant victory through one man's strength.

title: Grendel Walks the Wan Night
summary: Grendel strides through the night toward Heorot, where every warrior sleeps except one, Beowulf, who lies wakeful and angry, ready to await the battle's outcome.

title: Grendel Bursts Into Heorot
summary: Grendel bursts through Heorot's bolted door and devours one sleeping Geat, but Beowulf seizes his claw in a crushing grip, and Grendel, fearing for the first time and unable to flee, fights through a din that shakes the iron-bound hall while the terrified Danes listen outside.

title: Grendel's Shoulder Torn Away
summary: Beowulf's Geat followers draw their ancestral swords to defend him but cannot harm the spell-protected Grendel, until Beowulf's grip rips Grendel's shoulder apart, and the dying monster flees to his den in the moors.

title: The Hall Is Purged
summary: The Danes recognize Beowulf as having purged Heorot and made good his boast, ending their long sorrow, with Grendel's severed arm and shoulder displayed beneath the gabled roof as proof.

title: Warriors Trace Grendel's Bloody Trail
summary: At morning, warriors from far and near gather at Heorot to see Grendel's tracks, follow his dragging, death-marked trail to the mere, and find its waters boiling with his blood where he died and hell took his soul.

title: Riders Return, Praising Beowulf
summary: The old clansmen and young warriors ride home from the mere on white horses, praising Beowulf as the most worthy warrior and ruler under heaven without slighting Hrothgar, and race their gray steeds along the fair stretches of road.

title: The Thane Sings of Sigemund
summary: A king's thane, skilled in verse, sings of Beowulf's feat and adds the tale of Sigemund, who slew a dragon and won its hoard, then contrasts the failed king Heremod, banished and betrayed, while thanes judge Beowulf the kinder of the two.

title: Morning Procession to Heorot
summary: As the morning sun climbs, clansmen hurry to Heorot to see the wonder, and Hrothgar, crowned with glory, walks from the bride-bower with Wealhtheow and her maidens to the mead-hall.

title: Hrothgar Thanks the Victor
summary: Hrothgar stands at Heorot's steps, sees Grendel's hand under the roof, thanks God, adopts Beowulf as his son with a promise of endless wealth, and Beowulf replies that he wished Hrothgar had seen the fight, that Grendel broke free leaving his arm as pledge, and that the fiend now awaits God's doom.

title: Grendel's Claw Silences Unferth
summary: Unferth, once so boastful, falls silent as the assembled nobles gaze at Grendel's clawed hand beneath Heorot's roof, its nails hard as steel, and agree that no blade could have cut it from the spell-protected monster.

title: Heorot Garnished After the Fight
summary: Men and women hurry to cleanse and adorn Heorot with gold-bright wall hangings for the feast, though the hall's iron-braced hinges are broken and only its roof survived Grendel's flight, and the narrator observes that the doomed fiend will soon rest in death's bed.

title: Hrothgar's Banquet and Gifts
summary: At the feast in the restored Heorot, Hrothgar and Hrothulf sit among friendly Scyldings, and Hrothgar rewards Beowulf with a gold banner, helmet, breastplate, sword, and eight bridled horses, including his own jeweled battle-saddle, with rights over the steeds and weapons.

title: Hrothgar's Gifts and Wyrd's Wisdom
summary: At the ale-bench Hrothgar gives each of Beowulf's sea-crossing companions an heirloom and pays gold for the man Grendel murdered, while the narrator notes that God and Beowulf's courage averted worse slaughter and reflects on fate and foresight.

title: The Singer Recounts Finnsburh
summary: At the feast, Hrothgar's singer performs the Finnsburh lay: Hnaef falls in the Frisian slaughter, grieving Hildeburh loses brother and son, and the weakened Finn offers Hengest's Danes a sworn peace that forbids any taunt of the old slaughter on pain of the sword.

title: Hnaef's Pyre at Finnsburh
summary: As the singer's Finnsburh lay continues at the feast, oaths are sworn and gold heaped, Hnaef is laid on his pyre with the slain, and Hildeburh orders her own son burned beside her brother as she wails and the flames consume warriors of both peoples.

title: Hengest's Vengeance and the Queen's Return
summary: Hengest winters with Finn under the pact, longing for vengeance, until spring comes and Hun's sword death and Guthlaf and Oslaf's return bring the Danes' attack in which Finn is slain, his hall plundered, and Hildeburh taken home to the Danes.

title: Wealhtheow's Plea at the Feast
summary: After the Finnsburh lay, Queen Wealhtheow offers Hrothgar the cup, urges him to enjoy his gifts to the Geats but leave the realm to his own kin, voices trust that Hrothulf will honor her sons, then turns to where Hrethric and Hrothmund sit with Beowulf between them.

title: Wealhtheow Gifts Beowulf the Necklace
summary: Wealhtheow gives Beowulf a cup, arm-rings, corselet and the noblest necklace, blessing him and asking him to counsel her sons kindly and be helpful to them, then returns to her seat as the feast ends and the warriors bed down in Heorot, unaware of coming doom.

title: Warriors Bed Down Armed
summary: As the feast ends, the warriors lie down in Heorot with shields at their heads and helmets, spears and mail coats on the benches above them, as is their custom of staying battle-ready at home or abroad in case their king is threatened.

title: Grendel's Mother Avenges Her Son
summary: While Beowulf sleeps in another house, Grendel's mother bursts into Heorot to avenge her son, is driven off by the armed warriors, and flees to the moor with Hrothgar's dearest thane, whom she killed, and Grendel's blood-flecked hand, leaving the Danes and Geats in grief.

title: Beowulf Summoned at Daybreak
summary: At daybreak Beowulf is fetched in haste to his bower and goes with his earls to Hrothgar's chamber, where he greets the old king and asks whether the night passed in peace.

title: Hrothgar Names the Mere
summary: Hrothgar tells Beowulf that Aeschere is dead at the hands of Grendel's avenging mother, describes the monstrous pair and their dread mere, and asks Beowulf to hunt her there for a promised reward of ancient gold.

title: Beowulf Vows to Hunt Grendel's Mother
summary: Beowulf urges Hrothgar to avenge rather than mourn and vows that Grendel's mother cannot escape him anywhere, then leads the Danes along her trail over the moor to a gloomy wood above the mere, where the water is bloody and they find Aeschere's head.

title: Sea-Monster Slain at the Mere
summary: At the bloody mere the war-horn sounds and sea-serpents and nicors stir, and Beowulf shoots one through the heart with a bolt, after which the warriors drag the monster onto the headland with barbed boar-spears and look on it.

title: Beowulf Arms for the Mere
summary: At the mere's edge Beowulf dons his woven mail and gold-chained boar-crested helm and takes up Hrunting, the famed sword lent by Unferth, who dares not risk the waters himself and so forfeits his honor.

title: Beowulf's Farewell Charge to Hrothgar
summary: Before diving into the mere, Beowulf asks Hrothgar to stand as a father to him and guard his thanes if he dies, to send his gifts to Hygelac, and declares Unferth shall keep Hrunting, since he will win glory with it or die.

title: Into the Mere
summary: Without waiting for Hrothgar's reply, Beowulf plunges into the mere and sinks for most of a day before he reaches the bottom.

title: Seized in the Mere
summary: Grendel's mother senses the intruder at the mere's bottom, seizes Beowulf but cannot pierce his mail, and drags him through swarming sea-beasts into a dry, firelit hall beneath the water.

title: Blade Fails Against the Mere-Wife
summary: In the dry hall beneath the mere Beowulf strikes Grendel's mother with Hrunting, which fails to bite, so he flings it aside and wrestles her; she overthrows him and nearly stabs him with a short sword, but his mail turns the blade and he rises.

title: The Giant-Sword and Grendel's Head
summary: Beowulf seizes a giant-forged sword from the lair's armory and strikes down Grendel's mother, light fills the hall, and he finds Grendel's corpse and beheads it in vengeance for the raids on Heorot.

title: The Watchers Abandon the Mere
summary: Hrothgar and the old Danes see the mere churn and stain with blood, conclude Beowulf has died, and at the ninth hour Hrothgar leads the Danes home while Beowulf's Geat companions stay to stare at the water, hoping against belief.

title: Beowulf Returns With Grendel's Head
summary: Beowulf carries only Grendel's head and the jeweled hilt out of the lair after the giant sword melts, surfaces to his rejoicing Geat companions, and with fourteen Geats has the head hauled by the hair into Heorot, where the Danes look on in awe.

title: The Giant-Wrought Hilt Presented
summary: Beowulf recounts the underwater fight to Hrothgar, credits God for the giant sword after Hrunting failed, hands over the jeweled hilt, and assures the king Heorot is safe to sleep in again; Hrothgar studies the hilt's etched tale of the giants' flood, praises Beowulf, reaffirms his love, and warns him with the example of Heremod.

title: Hrothgar Warns Against Pride
summary: Hrothgar continues his warning to Beowulf, using Heremod's murder of his own companions and joyless solitary reign as a lesson, and then describes how God grants a man power and ease until pride wakes while his spirit's sentry sleeps and the murderer shoots.

title: Hrothgar's Warning Against Pride
summary: Hrothgar finishes his warning against pride, telling Beowulf that his strength will fade to age, sword, fire or death, recalls how Grendel shattered his own secure century of rule, thanks God for letting him live to see the bloody head, and bids Beowulf to the banquet bench with treasure to be shared at dawn.

title: Night Falls on the Banquet
summary: At dusk Beowulf accepts Hrothgar's invitation to the renewed banquet, then the old king and the weary Geat retire, and a hall-thane attends Beowulf's needs as a guest.

title: Dawn Departure, Hrunting Returned
summary: At dawn Beowulf wakes and the Geats ready to sail home; he has Hrunting returned to Unferth with thanks and no word against the blade despite its failure, then goes with his armed men to greet Hrothgar at the high-seat.

title: Hrothgar's Tearful Farewell to Beowulf
summary: Beowulf takes leave of Hrothgar, pledging Geat warriors to aid him and welcoming Hrethric at Hygelac's court, and Hrothgar praises his wisdom, foresees him as a worthy Geat king, pledges lasting peace and shared treasure between their peoples, gives him twelve gifts, then weeps as he embraces him, secretly longing to see him again.

title: Beowulf Walks to the Ship
summary: Glad of Hrothgar's gifts, Beowulf and his men cross the grass to the anchored ship, praising the blameless king whose splendid might was broken only by age.

title: The Geats Sail Home
summary: The coast-warden greets the departing Geats, Beowulf rewards the boat-guard with a gold-mounted sword, and the laden ship sails home across the sea to the Geatish cliffs, where the harbor-guard moors it and Beowulf has the treasure carried to Hygelac's nearby hall.

title: Hygd and Thryth: A Queenly Digression
summary: The narrator digresses to praise Hygd, Hygelac's young, wise, generous queen, contrasting her with the proud and murderous Thryth, who executed any man who looked her in the face until she married Offa, grew gentle and loyal, and made him renowned as a wise ruler.

title: Beowulf Returns to Hygelac's Hall
summary: Beowulf and his men hurry along the shore to Hygelac's hall, where Beowulf greets his lord, Hygd serves the mead, and Hygelac asks anxiously how the Danish venture went, recalling his own warnings against it and thanking God for Beowulf's safe return.

title: Beowulf Foretells the Heathobard Feud
summary: Beowulf tells Hygelac of his victory over Grendel and of Hrothgar's hall, then describes Freawaru's betrothal to Ingeld and predicts that an old Heathobard warrior will goad a young man over a Dane's captured heirloom sword until the peace breaks and Ingeld's war-hate returns.

title: Beowulf Recounts the Grendel Fight
summary: Beowulf, after doubting the Heathobards' peace, tells Hygelac how Grendel devoured Hondscio and seized him, how he tore off Grendel's arm so the monster fled to die, and how Hrothgar rewarded him with gold and a banquet where the aged king sang of yore.

title: Beowulf Recounts Killing Grendel's Mother
summary: Beowulf continues his report to Hygelac, telling how Grendel's mother avenged her son by killing Aeschere and carrying his body into the mere, how Hrothgar begged him to dive after her, how he beheaded her in the water after a struggle and barely survived, and how Hrothgar rewarded him with great gifts.

title: Gifts to Hygelac, Hrethel's Sword
summary: Beowulf gives Hygelac and Hygd the gifts from Hrothgar and Wealhtheow, then Hygelac, long despised by his Geats as slack, repays him with Hrethel's heirloom sword, seven thousand hides, a house and a high-seat.

title: The Dragon Wakes to Theft
summary: Narrator skips ahead: Hygelac and Heardred fall in battle, Beowulf becomes king and rules wisely fifty winters until a dragon guarding a barrow hoard begins to rage after a stranger steals a golden goblet while it sleeps, dooming prince and people to pay for its wrath.

title: The Fugitive Steals the Cup
summary: A fugitive thane, driven by peril rather than choice, takes shelter in the dragon's barrow, is terrified by what he sees, but rallies and takes a cup from the hoard before fleeing.

title: The Last Survivor's Lament
summary: The last survivor of a clan wiped out in battle seals the heirlooms and gold in a seaside barrow and, in a lament, gives them back to the earth because no one remains to wield or polish them.

title: The Dragon Claims the Hoard
summary: After the last survivor dies lamenting, the twilight-flying fire-dragon finds the open hoard, guards it in the earth for three hundred winters, and its wrath is roused when a man brings a costly cup to his lord and pleads for him.

title: The Dragon Wakes to Theft
summary: The fugitive's theft is completed and his lord receives the cup; the dragon wakes, follows the thief's footprints by its head, circles the barrow in rage, finds no one, discovers the cup is gone from its hoard, and waits furiously for evening to take fiery vengeance.

title: The Dragon Flies Out in Flame
summary: When evening falls as it has awaited, the enraged dragon abandons its barrow wall and flies out wrapped in flame, beginning a terror for the people that will end in their lord's doom.

title: The Dragon's Night of Fire
summary: The dragon burns the Geatish homes and lands through the night, leaving nothing living, then retreats to its barrow at dawn, trusting in its lair and fire, a trust the narrator calls vain.

title: Beowulf Learns and Plans Vengeance
summary: Beowulf learns the dragon has burned his royal hall, fears he has angered God, and has an iron shield forged to face the dragon alone, recalling his past battles and how he came to rule the Geats.

title: Thirteen Men Seek the Dragon
summary: Beowulf, enraged, sets out with eleven companions to find the dragon, forced to take the reluctant, cringing fugitive thane as thirteenth man and guide, who leads them to the treasure-filled barrow by the sea where the dragon lurks.

title: Beowulf Speaks of Hrethel's Grief
summary: Seated on the headland above the dragon's barrow, the gloomy, death-foreboding Beowulf addresses his companions and begins recounting his youth under Hrethel, including how Haethcyn accidentally killed Herebeald and left the old king in unavenged grief.

title: Hrethel's Grief and Geatish Wars
summary: Beowulf, on the headland, continues his recollection: Hrethel, unable to avenge Herebeald's death, died of grief, then Swedish-Geatish war broke out under Ongentheow's sons, Haethcyn fell, and Eofor killed Ongentheow in vengeance.

title: Beowulf's Last Battle-Vow
summary: Beowulf finishes recalling his loyal service to Hygelac, including killing Daeghrefn bare-handed, then makes his last battle-vow, explains he brings armor against the dragon's fire and poison, and orders his companions to wait at the barrow while he fights alone to win the hoard or die.

title: Beowulf Faces the Dragon
summary: Beowulf finds the barrow's arch and its fire-hot stream, roars a challenge that rouses the dragon, and fights it alone with shield and heirloom sword, but the blade fails against the dragon and the dragon's flames drive him back before the two close again.

title: Companions Flee, Wiglaf Remains
summary: As the dragon revives and engulfs Beowulf in flames, his eleven companions flee to the woods to save their lives, but one, Wiglaf, stays, his kinship-bound heart troubled.

title: Wiglaf Arms and Rallies Comrades
summary: Wiglaf, seeing Beowulf hard pressed by the dragon's fire, seizes his shield and his father's inherited sword from Eanmund, and urges the fleeing comrades to honor their oaths and help their lord, declaring he would rather burn beside the king and offering his own arms to shield them both.

title: Wiglaf Stands With Beowulf
summary: Wiglaf reaches Beowulf through the battle-reek and urges him to defend his life, but the dragon returns in flame burning Wiglaf's shield so he shelters behind Beowulf's, then Beowulf's sword Naegling shatters on the dragon's head and the dragon seizes his neck, drenching him in blood.

title: Wiglaf Aids Beowulf Against Dragon
summary: Wiglaf strikes the dragon lower with his sword, burning his hand, and Beowulf then draws his war-knife and helps kill it, but Beowulf's poisoned wound swells, he sits by the barrow wall as Wiglaf bathes him, and dying without an heir he sends Wiglaf to view the hoard.

title: Wiglaf Plunders the Dragon's Hoard
summary: Wiglaf enters the dragon's barrow in his mail-coat at the dying Beowulf's command, finds the dead dragon gone and the hoard of gold, vessels, arm-rings and a gold banner unguarded, loads himself with treasure and the banner, and hurries back fearing Beowulf may already be dead.

title: Beowulf's Last Words
summary: Wiglaf returns with the hoard and revives the dying Beowulf, who thanks God for the treasure won for his people, orders a headland barrow raised as his memorial, gives Wiglaf his collar, helmet, breastplate and ring as the last of the Waegmundings, and dies.

title: Wiglaf Beholds Fallen King and Dragon
summary: Wiglaf looks on his dead lord Beowulf lying lifeless beside the fallen dragon, and the narrator reflects that few men dare face such a hoard-guarding poison-foe and that Beowulf paid with his life for the treasure while both combatants met their end.

title: Wiglaf Shames the Faithless Cowards
summary: The ten oath-breaking companions slink back from the wood with their shields to find Beowulf dead and Wiglaf failing to revive him, and Wiglaf bitterly rebukes them, declaring they will lose gifts, land and honor and that death is better than a life of shame.

title: The Herald Proclaims the King's Fall
summary: The herald rides up to the cliff fort where the anxious earls have waited all morning, announces that Beowulf and the dragon lie dead with Wiglaf keeping watch, warns that the king's fall will bring war from Franks, Frisians and Swedes, and begins recounting the history of those feuds beginning with Hygelac's fatal Frisian raid.

title: Ongentheow Besieges the Ravenswood Survivors
summary: The herald continues his history of the Swedish feud, recounting how Ongentheow besieged the wounded Geats at Ravenswood all night, threatening them with death and the gallows, until Hygelac's horn sounded at dawn and brought rescue.

title: Ongentheow's Fall and Eofor's Reward
summary: The herald concludes his account of the Swedish feud: Ongentheow retreats to his fort, is pursued by Hygelac's Geats, and is slain by Eofor, whom Hygelac rewards with vast treasure and his only daughter.

title: The Messenger's Warning and Pyre
summary: The herald closes his account by predicting Swedish revenge once Beowulf's death is known, urges the earls to hurry to the body and bear it to the pyre where the whole hoard will burn with him, and foretells exile, cold spears and carrion birds feasting on the slain.

title: The King and the Dragon, Dead
summary: Led by the herald's tidings, the sorrowing Geat warriors climb the Cliff-of-Eagles and find Beowulf dead beside the fifty-measure dragon and its rust-eaten, spell-bound hoard, which no man could touch unless God chose to open it.

title: Wiglaf Rebukes the Retainers
summary: Wiglaf addresses the assembled Geat warriors at the barrow, recounting how Beowulf's fatal venture was against their counsel, relaying the dying king's order for a high headland barrow, and urging them to view the hoard and prepare the bier to bear him to rest.

title: Wiglaf Calls for Funeral Wood
summary: Wiglaf commands the Geat landholders to bring firewood from across their lands for Beowulf's funeral pyre, where fire will consume the warrior who stood firm beneath storms of arrows.

title: Looting the Dragon's Hoard
summary: Wiglaf picks seven of the best thanes and leads them with a torch into the barrow, where they find the hoard unguarded, haul it out, push the dragon's corpse over the cliff into the sea, load the gold on a wain, and carry Beowulf to Hrones-Ness.

title: The Geats Burn Their King
summary: The Geats build a pyre hung with helmets and war-gear, lay Beowulf upon it and light the vast blaze amid weeping, while an old Geatish widow sings her lament and dreads the coming days of death, battle and shame.

title: The Geats Raise Beowulf's Barrow
summary: The Weders spend ten days raising a high, sea-visible barrow on the headland around the pyre's embers, then bury the dragon's hoard inside it, returning the gold to the earth where it lies as useless to men as before.

title: The Twelve Riders' Lament
summary: Twelve noble-born warriors ride around Beowulf's barrow, chanting a dirge and praising his lordship and deeds, affirming that men should honor and love their lord when he departs this life.

title: The Geats Praise Their Fallen King
summary: The Geats close their mourning for Beowulf, declaring that of all the kings of earth he was the mildest, most beloved, kindest to his kin and keenest for praise.
